title: Transitivity
definition: Traditionally, transitivity is treated as a categorical property of a clause: a verb either takes an [term:patient]-like object, giving a transitive clause with [term:agent] (A) and object (O) arguments, or it does not, giving an intransitive clause with a single (S) argument. On this view a clause is simply transitive or intransitive, and the notion is understood as an activity 'carried over' or 'transferred' from an [term:agent] to a [term:patient]. Hopper & Thompson (1980) argue this binary picture is too coarse. They reanalyze Transitivity as a scalar property built from ten components that co-vary across languages, each ranging from a 'high' to a 'low' value: (A) participants — two or more (A and O) vs. one; (B) kinesis — action vs. non-action (something happens to Sally in *I hugged Sally*, but not in *I like Sally*); (C) aspect — telic vs. atelic (*I ate it up* vs. *I am eating it*); (D) punctuality — punctual vs. non-punctual (*kick* vs. *carry*); (E) volitionality — volitional vs. non-volitional (*I wrote your name* vs. *I forgot your name*); (F) affirmation — affirmative vs. negative; (G) mode — realis vs. irrealis; (H) agency — A high vs. low in potency (*George startled me* vs. *The picture startled me*); (I) [term:affectedness] of O — totally affected vs. not affected (*I drank up the milk* vs. *I drank some of the milk*); and (J) [term:individuation] of O — highly individuated vs. non-individuated, itself cashed out along several sub-scales (proper vs. common, human/animate vs. inanimate, concrete vs. abstract, singular vs. plural, count vs. mass, referential/definite vs. non-referential). A clause is not simply transitive or intransitive but more or less Transitive depending on how many of these components fall in the 'high' column; a clause high on every parameter exhibits CARDINAL Transitivity. Hopper & Thompson further argue these grammatical and semantic components are not arbitrary: they cluster together because Transitivity has a discourse function, with high-Transitivity clauses correlating with foregrounded, plot-advancing material and low-Transitivity clauses with backgrounded description.

examples.title: Low transitivity (English)
examples.notes: A stative, non-punctual, non-volitional predicate with a non-individuated (mass, non-referential) object — low on kinesis, punctuality, volitionality, and individuation of O.

examples.title: High transitivity (English)
examples.notes: Action, telic, punctual, volitional predicate with a totally affected, highly individuated (referential, animate, proper) object — high on nearly every parameter, close to cardinal Transitivity.

examples.title: Near-zero transitivity (English)
examples.translation: There were no stars in the sky.
examples.notes: Only one participant, negative, with a non-referential O — has no feature in the 'high' column except realis mode.

examples.title: Individuation of O driving morphology: differential object marking (Spanish)
examples.translation: Vi a Juan. ('I saw Juan.') vs. Vi la mesa. ('I saw the table.')
examples.notes: Spanish differential object marking makes parameter J concrete: the preposition-derived marker a appears on the object only when it is animate and specific/referential — a highly individuated O — and is absent for the inanimate, equally definite la mesa. The same verb, the same event structure, but individuation of O alone determines whether the object is morphologically marked.
